item.title: Nasdaq 100 posts worst week since March 2020
item.description:
U.S. stocks closed sharply lower Friday, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 5.61% on the day and 10.43% for the week, its worst since March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28%, wiping out its gains for the year, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.70% for its seventh straight decline. The Dow lost 950 points.

Nvidia fell 14.01% to $125.53 after Reuters reported that the SEC was probing its accounting. The selling reached across the AI trade, from the companies designing chips to the ones supplying memory, optical gear and power. Treasuries caught a bid, with the 10-year yield down 12 basis points to 4.93%. Even with yields moving lower, tech shares remained under pressure.

U.S. closing levels

  • Dow Industrial Average −950.10 points (−1.93%) to 48,151.82. Week −8.03%.
  • S&P 500 −265.44 points (−3.70%) to 6,910.39. Week −8.61%.
  • Nasdaq Composite −1,261.47 points (−5.28%) to 22,617.73. Week −10.02%.
  • Russell 2000 −73.32 points (−2.76%) to 2,581.79. Week −7.48%.
  • Nasdaq 100 −1,488.07 points (−5.61%) to 25,028.98. Week −10.43%.

The Dow had its worst week since March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite’s 10.02% loss was in line with its worst week in the spring 2025 selloff, while the S&P 500 had its worst week since that stretch. Friday’s breadth showed how far the selling spread. Nearly five Nasdaq stocks fell for every one that rose, and S&P 500 decliners outnumbered advancers 357 to 125.

The two Nasdaq levels to watch next week

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 22,617.73, just 99.82 points above its 100-week moving average at 22,517.91. The Nasdaq 100 finished at 25,028.98, just 111.63 points above its own 100-week moving average at 24,917.35. Both cushions are less than 0.5%.

Sellers have the short-term bias after a week like this. The two moving averages give buyers a place to lean against, but they need to hold those levels and put some distance between price and support. If both indices get below their averages and stay below, the bearish bias increases. On a rebound, I’d watch whether Nasdaq breadth improves alongside the indices.

Double-digit losses across the AI trade

Twenty-two names on the AI and chip watchlist fell more than 10% Friday, including the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, which dropped 10.60%. The losses reached across the AI buildout.

  • AI cloud and infrastructure — Nebius −16.11%, CoreWeave −12.02%.
  • Chip design and compute — Arm −14.09%, Nvidia −14.01%, AMD −13.25%, Broadcom −12.19%.
  • Memory and storage — SanDisk −16.05%, Micron −13.89%, Western Digital −12.02%.
  • Networking and optics — Credo −15.20%, Lumentum −13.94%, Coherent −12.90%, Arista Networks −11.57%.
  • Power and chipmaking equipment — Bloom Energy −15.26%, Applied Materials −10.71%, KLA −10.33%, Lam Research −10.02%.

Trading education. Let support define your risk

If you’re leaning against a weekly moving average, decide what would invalidate the trade before you enter. A quick dip followed by a reclaim can tell you sellers had their shot and missed. A break followed by a failed rally back above the average tells you sellers are defending the level. The same moving average can help you define risk in either direction.

item.title: AUDUSD is the biggest mover of the major currencies this week. The price falls -2.30% for the week.
item.description:
The AUDUSD is the weakest of the major currencies vs the greenback. It fell -2.3%.  The price has now fallen for 10 consecutive days. That move has taken the price from a high on November 10 at 0.69296 to the low today at 0.6609 or -320 pips.  

The 320-pip slide in AUDUSD started with a repricing of Fed rate expectations and picked up steam as Australia’s jobs market weakened and the global equity selloff deepened. The Aussie’s 2.30% decline this week, the largest of the seven majors you tracked against the USD, also reflected weakness against other currencies, including the yen and euro.

  • Hot US inflation got the USD rally going. The November 10 CPI report showed prices rising 0.4% month over month vs. 0.3% expected. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point December hike should be considered. That pushed traders to price in a more aggressive Fed and helped lift the dollar index to its highest level since April 2025. investing.com
  • Australia’s jobs report took away rate support for the Aussie. Australia lost 43,500 jobs in October and unemployment rose to 4.9%, the highest in five years. The RBA had just raised its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3, but after the jobs report, swaps dropped bets on another hike and priced in easing for 2027. Australian three-year yields fell 17 basis points on Thursday. That was the clearest domestic catalyst for the latest leg lower. Australian Bureau of Statistics
  • The AI-led equity selloff kept pressure on the Aussie. Investors pulled back from risk as tech stocks sold off, while copper and gold also came under pressure. AUDUSD remained under pressure Friday even as US Treasury yields fell and the broader dollar rally paused. The Aussie’s losses against the yen and euro reinforced the picture of broad AUD selling.
  • Weak Chinese data added to the growth concerns. October industrial production rose 4.8% year over year vs. 5.3% expected, while retail sales rose 0.4% vs. 0.8% expected and property investment continued to contract sharply. China is Australia’s largest trading partner and a major buyer of its iron ore, so weaker Chinese activity added to concerns about demand for Australian exports.

On the daily chart, AUDUSD broke below 0.6751 earlier this week, taking out the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the 2025 low. Sellers kept the pressure on, pushing through swing levels at 0.6706 and 0.66588 in succession.

The next downside target is 0.65905, the 50% retracement of that same rally. On a rebound, 0.66588 is the first barometer for buyers. Getting back above that level would take some of the pressure off.

Drilling down to the hourly chart, the AUDUSD selloff started on November 2 with a break below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages. The pair corrected higher on November 4, but by November 5 it was back below both averages. The price has stayed below the lower 100-hour MA ever since.

That 100-hour MA now comes in at 0.67017 and is the first barometer for buyers. They need to get and stay above it to begin to wrestle back some control. If they can do that, the next target is 0.6730, the 38.2% retracement of the move down from the November 9 high. Above that, the 200-hour MA at 0.67586 is the next hurdle.

Until buyers can get and stay above 0.67017, the sellers remain in control on the hourly chart

item.title: Nvidia falls after SEC probe on potential accounting issues
item.description:
Shares of Nvidia are trading down $17.25 at $128.80. It low reached $128.66. That is the lowest level going back to May 14, 2025.

Technically the price fell below the 61.8% retracement of the move up from the 2025 low at $146.50. It is now approaching its 200 week moving average at $124.16.

The share price is now down -21% on the week which is its worst week since October 2008 when shares tumbled by -24.58%. 

If the buyer is looking to put a toe in the water, the 200 week moving average at $124.15 is a level that traders could potentially lean against with a stop on a break below.

The most recent move to the downside today came after reports of a SEC probe into potential accounting issues for the firm. Shares were already fragile and that was another straw on the camels back. Did it break the back?  We will see if the selling continues below the 200 week MA.  

Recall, that Nvidia reported fiscal Q3 2027 results on Tuesday, Nov. 17, its first earnings release since Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO. Revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, driven by the data center business and the rollout of its Vera Rubin platform. investor.nvidia.com

  • Adjusted EPS — $2.68 vs. $2.49 expected (BEAT), up 111% year over year.
  • Revenue — $115.84 billion vs. $109.28 billion expected (BEAT), up 103% year over year and 20% from the prior quarter.
  • Data center revenue — $107.6 billion, up 110% year over year and 21% from the prior quarter. It accounted for roughly 93% of total sales.
  • Q4 outlook — Nvidia sees revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, versus Wall Street’s estimate of just over $125 billion. The quarter includes an extra week, and the forecast assumes zero data center compute revenue from China. Gross margin is expected to ease to 71%–72% from 74.9% on an adjusted basis in Q3.

On the call, interim CEO Colette Kress raised Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75% from 70%, citing strong demand and additional supply. The stock initially rallied after hours, then gave back the gain and closed the next session down 2.9% at $150.96..

Looking at the broad market, the NASDAQ composite Index is trading at 22,876 down 1003 points or -4.20%. It is approaching its 100 week moving average at 22520.35. It is also below its closing level for 2025 at 23242.

item.title: Fed’s Cook says monetary policy isn’t restrictive enough
item.description:
The Fed’s Cook weighed in on inflation, the labor market and the need for tighter monetary policy in remarks that crossed the wires.

  • Fed’s current monetary policy stance is not providing needed restraint.
  • September’s interest rate hike was not enough to curtail high inflation.
  • High inflation does not give U.S. central bank space to be patient.
  • Holding off on rate hikes increases risk that inflation will embed in economy.
  • Data since September points to need for tighter monetary policy.
  • Current level of inflation is of “great concern.”
  • U.S. economic growth is strong, labor market is healthy and stable.
  • Embedded inflation will require more aggressive Fed response.
  • Financial conditions are too accommodative right now.
  • Tariff impact on inflation has faded.
  • Little evidence AI is weighing on job market so far.

Analysis

These are hawkish comments from Cook. In her view, the September hike didn’t deliver enough restraint, and financial conditions are still too easy. With growth strong and the labor market holding up, she sees room for the Fed to tighten further. She also says tariffs’ impact on inflation has faded, yet the current level of inflation remains a concern.

For traders, the strongest policy signal is how Cook frames the cost of waiting. If inflation becomes embedded, she thinks the Fed will have to respond more aggressively. That puts more weight on the next inflation readings and whether they give the Fed any room to hold rates steady.

Let's face it, the Fed kept rates unchanged at the October meeting.   The minutes suggested a more hawkish bias. The election likely was influence.  The Fed officials seem to suggest that inflation is not getting better but worse.  

Meanwhile the US yields are moving lower with the shorter end of the yield curve down -14 basis points at 4.64%. The 10 year is down -11.62 basis points at 4.935%. For the 2 year, the low yield in November reached 4.448%. So the yield is still well above that level. As far as Fed expectations, in December the chance for remaining unchanged actually increased to 4.2%. The chance for a 50 basis point hike is now 0% while the chance of a 25 basis point hike is 95.8%.

Stocks continue to get hammered with the NASDAQ composite down -3.51% in the NASDAQ 100 down -3.76%.

Pres. Trump press conference is beginning now.

item.title: Could Jensen Huang end up at SpaceX? Dan Ives thinks he could work alongside Elon Musk
item.description:
SpaceX has already lined up about $40 billion in financing for AI computing equipment, including next-generation Nvidia chips.

In a Bloomberg interview about 30 minutes ago, tech analyst Dan Ives was asked where Jensen Huang might be a year from now. His answer was SpaceX. Ives floated the possibility that the Nvidia co-founder could become co-CEO alongside Elon Musk, framing it as his personal prediction.

Asked where Jensen Huang might be a year from now, tech analyst Dan Ives had a surprising answer: SpaceX. Ives floated the possibility that the Nvidia co-founder could become co-CEO alongside Elon Musk. That was Ives’ personal prediction. SpaceX still lists Musk as its sole CEO.

There’s a business reason the idea is worth a look. In October, SpaceX said it had secured a financing commitment of about $40 billion for chips and related equipment, including Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips. Those chips are earmarked for data centers on Earth. Huang spent decades building the business that supplies the kind of computing power SpaceX is now buying at scale.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12, and CFO Colette Kress took over as interim CEO. On Thursday, California’s attorney general issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia seeking information about whether advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether the company misled investors. For Nvidia shareholders, the next developments to watch are the company’s choice of a permanent CEO and what it discloses about the investigation.

The break below $3,610.01 keeps sellers in control

On the downside, the price is now testing the upper end of the $3,433.49 to $3,550.21 swing area. There were several stalls in that area in 2025 before buyers finally broke through and extended the rally. The question now is whether buyers show up on the way back down.

If sellers can get and stay below that level, the next major retracement target on the daily chart comes in at $3,140.67. That’s the 61.8% retracement of the move up from the 2022 low.

For now, the swing area gives buyers a place to make a play and define their risk. A bounce from the area would be a start. Getting back above $3,610.01 and holding it is what would give buyers more room to work.

The University of Michigan’s monthly survey asks U.S. households about current economic conditions, the outlook and where they expect inflation to go. item.title: The stock market's wealth effect: why it matters even if you don't own stocks
item.description:
Equity market movements can have a significant impact on the economy through the so-called "wealth effect", changes in financial conditions and the influence on corporate investment and hiring decisions.

People can be affected by a stock market rally or selloff, even if they don't own stocks. Companies rely on financial markets to raise capital, finance expansions, make acquisitions and attract investment. When equity markets rise or collapse, the consequences can eventually reach workers, consumers and businesses across the economy.

Households wealth

The most straightforward transmission channel is the household wealth effect. When stock prices rise, households with equity exposure become wealthier, at least on paper. This includes people holding individual stocks, ETFs and mutual funds, as well as workers with retirement accounts and pension investments.

As their portfolios appreciate, households may feel more financially secure and become more comfortable increasing consumption. They might purchase a new car, renovate their homes, travel more frequently or increase discretionary spending. This is the positive wealth effect as rising asset prices support consumer confidence and spending, providing an additional boost to economic growth.

The reverse is also true. When stock prices fall sharply, households suffer a decline in financial wealth. Even when their employment and current income remain unchanged, they may become more cautious, postpone large purchases and increase precautionary savings. This negative wealth effect can weigh on consumption and eventually translate into weaker economic activity.

Wealthier households generally hold a disproportionate share of equities and tend to spend a smaller proportion of each additional dollar of wealth than lower-income households. Nevertheless, large and prolonged changes in equity prices can have meaningful aggregate effects on consumer demand.

Equity financing

The other important transmission mechanism is financing. The stock market plays an important role in determining how easily and cheaply companies can raise capital. Consider a company planning to expand its operations, build a new factory, invest in technology or hire additional employees. It may need external financing to execute those plans.

When equity valuations are high, issuing new shares becomes more attractive because the company can raise more capital while giving away a smaller ownership stake. A higher stock price can also make acquisitions easier by allowing companies to use their shares as a more valuable form of payment. Moreover, higher valuations can reduce the effective cost of equity financing and improve a company's ability to attract investors.

The opposite happens when stock prices collapse. Raising capital through equity issuance becomes more expensive in terms of dilution, investors become more reluctant to provide funding, and companies may postpone expansion plans.

This is closely related to the economic concept of Tobin's Q, which compares a company's market valuation with the replacement cost of its assets. When market valuations are high relative to the cost of building equivalent productive assets, investment becomes more attractive. When valuations are depressed, the incentive to invest can weaken.

Of course, companies do not finance all their investments through stock issuance. Internal cash flows, bank loans and corporate bonds remain important sources of funding. However, equity valuations influence the overall cost and availability of capital. And this is where the effects start reaching people who have never invested in the stock market.

Imagine a publicly listed company whose share price falls 40% following a prolonged stock market selloff. The company might not immediately face financial distress, but its ability to raise fresh equity capital has deteriorated. Management may become more cautious about future investments, acquisitions and expansion plans.

Instead of opening new facilities, increasing production capacity or hiring additional workers, the company might decide to preserve cash and delay projects. Its suppliers could subsequently receive fewer orders. Contractors might lose business. Hiring plans could be scaled back, while employees could face weaker wage growth or even layoffs. The effects can spread across the supply chain and eventually impact businesses that have nothing to do with the stock market.

In other words, a stock market selloff can eventually translate into fewer investments, weaker hiring and slower wage growth across the economy, including among people who do not own any assets.

Why central banks care about the stock market

These transmission mechanisms help explain why central banks pay attention to equity market movements, even though their mandates do not include supporting stock prices. Central banks care about the impact of financial conditions on inflation and economic activity.

Consider two scenarios. In the first, equities rally strongly, credit spreads narrow and risk appetite improves. Households feel wealthier, companies find it easier to finance expansion and financial conditions become more accommodative. This can support demand and potentially make the fight against inflation more difficult.

In the second, equities suffer a prolonged selloff, credit spreads widen and financing becomes more restrictive. Consumption and investment may weaken, reducing demand and easing inflationary pressures. In this second scenario, the tightening in financial conditions could partially do the work of monetary policy itself, potentially reducing the need for further interest rate increases.

Growth expectations matter

The stock market is forward-looking and reacts to changes in economic expectations. If the market anticipates a recession, stock prices may fall well before the weakness becomes visible in employment, consumption or economic data. In that case, the stock market selloff is partly a reflection of deteriorating economic expectations rather than the cause of the slowdown.

However, once valuations decline, the financial and wealth effects described above can reinforce the initial deterioration. This can create a negative feedback loop where expectations of weaker growth trigger a selloff, the selloff tightens financial conditions, tighter financial conditions weigh on consumption and investment, and the resulting economic weakness validates the original bearish expectations.

The same mechanism works in the opposite direction during periods of improving sentiment. A rally driven by better growth expectations can support household wealth, corporate financing and investment, helping reinforce the economic recovery. This is the basic idea behind Soros's theory of reflexivity.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Is ANT stock a buy or sell?
item.description:
Anthropic stock is sliding toward $83. Could Wall Street have a reason to defend its IPO price?

Anthropic shares have surrendered much of their spectacular IPO debut as the AI sector comes under pressure. A closer examination of the company's financing history, SEC disclosures and overnight trading reveals why $83 could become an important test, although institutional support is far from guaranteed.

Anthropic (NASDAQ: ANT) shares were trading around $87.63 in Friday's premarket session on November 20, 2026, down approximately 9.8% from Thursday's closing price of $97.17.

The decline raises an interesting question for traders and investors: Could the institutions involved in the biggest IPO in history have an incentive to defend Anthropic's $83 offering price?

There are reasons to pay particular attention to that level. But the latest price action also suggests that buyers have not yet regained control.

From $115 to below $88 in less than a day

Anthropic's first trading session on November 19 began with extraordinary enthusiasm.

The Claude AI developer priced its IPO at $83 per share, above its original $70-$78 marketing range, raising approximately $81.34 billion through the public offering. That implied a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion.

The shares opened at $111.50, reached $115.10 and eventually closed at $97.17.

Although that closing price represented a 17.1% gain over the offering price, investors buying near the first-day high had already experienced a substantial reversal.

By Friday's premarket low near $87.31, the stock had surrendered approximately 24% from Thursday's peak.

This is an important distinction between a successful IPO for investors who received shares at $83 and the experience of investors buying the stock after public trading began.

Someone purchasing shares at the $111.50 opening price would already be facing a paper loss of approximately 21% at the $87.63 premarket quote, even though IPO participants allocated shares at $83 would still be ahead.

What the five-minute chart reveals about the overnight selloff

The detailed overnight price action adds another useful observation.

Anthropic did not simply fall in one uninterrupted move from Thursday's close.

During the evening and overnight session, the stock repeatedly attempted to stabilize around $90-$92. Several rebounds occurred, including a recovery toward $92.41 around 3:30 a.m. Eastern Time and another move toward $92 around 5:30 a.m.

Neither attempt produced a sustained recovery.

More importantly, the character of the decline changed during the final hour of the observed premarket period.

Around 6:25 a.m. Eastern, the stock was still trading near $90.67. By approximately 6:30 a.m., it had broken lower, and subsequent selling carried it toward $87.31 by 7:20 a.m.

That represents a decline of approximately 3.7% from the earlier $90.67 reference to the low in less than an hour.

The new information here is that repeated attempts to stabilize were eventually followed by an accelerating decline, rather than the formation of a convincing recovery.

This does not establish who was selling. Extended-hours trading can also be less liquid and more volatile than the regular Nasdaq session.

Nevertheless, it makes the next trading session particularly interesting.

The $90-$91 area, which repeatedly attracted attempted recoveries overnight, could become a useful near-term reference if buyers try to regain control. The previous regular-session low at $92.72 is another obstacle above.

Why the $83 IPO price matters to institutional investors

Anthropic's final SEC prospectus contains a detail that makes the $83 offering price especially relevant.

Morgan Stanley, acting as stabilization agent for the underwriting syndicate, is permitted to undertake certain transactions intended to stabilize or support the market price following the offering.

The underwriting agreement also provides an option to purchase up to 147 million additional shares at the IPO price of $83, exercisable for 30 days.

Here is why that matters.

Underwriters sometimes sell additional shares as part of an IPO distribution, creating a short position that they subsequently need to cover.

If the stock trades below the offering price, purchasing shares in the open market may become more attractive than exercising the option to buy additional shares at $83.

Those purchases can potentially support the share price.

But there is no obligation for the underwriters to defend $83 or any other price. The prospectus explicitly allows stabilization activities to end at any time.

Therefore, $83 is a documented institutional reference price, not a guaranteed market floor.

The other $26 billion reason to watch $83

The public IPO was accompanied by a separate $26 billion strategic private placement at the same $83 price.

According to Anthropic's SEC filings, the investors included:

  • Google and Nvidia, each committing approximately $10 billion.

  • AMD, committing approximately $2.5 billion.

  • Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft, each committing approximately $1 billion.

  • TSMC, committing approximately $500 million.

These commitments make $83 a significant economic reference for some of the world's largest technology companies.

However, these investors may view their Anthropic stakes as long-term strategic investments associated with cloud computing, AI infrastructure and commercial relationships.

A strategic investor's entry price does not necessarily create an incentive to intervene in the secondary market whenever the stock falls.

There is another counterweight. The prospectus indicates that up to 315 million shares could become eligible for sale beginning shortly after the offering, subject to applicable conditions and restrictions. Eligibility does not establish that any of these shares have actually been sold, but it illustrates why potential supply must also be considered.

What about Anthropic's valuation before the IPO?

Another useful reference comes from Anthropic's final major private financing.

In May 2026, the company announced a $65 billion Series H funding round at a post-money valuation of approximately $965 billion.

The financing included preferred shares purchased at $589.0095 each. After accounting for the applicable conversion into ten common shares, the equivalent purchase price was approximately $58.90 per common share.

That is substantially below the $83 IPO price.

Consequently, investors participating in that private round may still have considerable unrealized gains, even if Anthropic were to trade below its public offering price. Their securities, rights and liquidity restrictions may also differ from those of ordinary public shareholders.

This creates an important distinction:

The $83 level is relevant to new IPO participants and the underwriting arrangements. The approximately $58.90 equivalent price represents an earlier private financing cost basis, not immediate technical support.

Neither establishes what Anthropic must be worth in the public market today.

Anthropic stock: The important prices to watch next

$92.72: The first trading day's low

Friday's premarket decline has already moved beneath this level. A recovery above it, followed by sustained trading, would be a more constructive indication that buyers are rebuilding confidence.

$90-$91: An overnight stabilization area that weakened

Several attempted rebounds occurred around this area before the sharper decline. If ANT recovers, whether it can regain and hold this territory may provide an earlier indication of improving short-term demand.

$83: The central IPO price reference

This is the most important level in the institutional-support discussion. It is the actual price paid by public IPO participants and the reference price for the concurrent strategic placement and underwriting option.

A recovery after testing this level would be worth watching. But a brief touch and rebound would not, by itself, prove institutional buying or establish durable support.

$70-$78: The original IPO marketing range

If $83 fails, the original offering range becomes a relevant historical valuation reference. These were proposed pricing levels before the actual offering, however, and should not automatically be treated as established technical support.

What would suggest that $83 is being defended?

The more constructive scenario would involve ANT approaching the IPO price, experiencing a slowing decline and subsequently recovering with sustained buying interest.

A successful retest, followed by recovery through some of the previously lost trading areas, would add evidence that market participants are willing to accept prices above the offering level.

The less constructive scenario would involve the stock falling below $83, failing to reclaim it and continuing lower.

That would raise questions about whether the enormous institutional commitments made around the IPO are translating into meaningful secondary-market demand.

It is also possible for underwriting-related purchases to temporarily slow a decline without generating a lasting recovery. Once those purchases end, independent investors must provide sufficient demand.

This distinction matters particularly because the broader AI sector is experiencing selling pressure. As investingLive reported during Thursday's session, Anthropic's record IPO did not prevent weakness across major US equity indices.

The important lesson for investors

Anthropic's $83 offering price deserves attention because it represents a substantial, documented financial transaction involving major institutions, technology companies and Wall Street underwriters.

It is more meaningful than an arbitrary round number on a chart.

But a reason for institutions to care about a price is not proof that they will defend it.

For traders, the more useful question is whether the market begins demonstrating genuine demand as ANT approaches this level.

For longer-term investors, another question is equally important: does Anthropic's business outlook justify its valuation independently of where the IPO was priced?

These are two different considerations, and both deserve attention.

At the observed premarket price near $87.63, the $83 offering price was only about 5.3% lower. That makes the potential test relevant, but not inevitable.

Patience may be particularly valuable in a newly listed stock experiencing large price swings. An apparently attractive price can become considerably less attractive if selling pressure continues.

Market analysis reflects the November 20, 2026 premarket snapshot around 7:24 a.m. Eastern Time, before the US regular trading session. Price levels are conditional observations, not guaranteed support or trade recommendations.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Is Nvidia stock a buy or sell? My opinion and 'buy the dip' trade plan
item.description:
Nvidia stock keeps falling despite record sales. Here's a patient plan for buying the dip

Even after another quarter of extraordinary revenue growth, Nvidia shares remain under pressure. For investors considering the decline an opportunity, this illustrative strategy identifies three potential buying prices, four recovery targets and a risk-management plan that does not depend on predicting the exact bottom.

Nvidia (NVDA) presents investors with a difficult choice. The company continues to deliver exceptional growth, yet its shares have fallen sharply. Is this an opportunity to buy at a more attractive price, or could further losses lie ahead?

Rather than guessing where the bottom will be, one approach is to prepare a staged buying strategy with predefined risk and profit targets.

Nvidia's business is growing, but its stock tells another story

On November 17, Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year, and projected approximately $130 billion in revenue for the following quarter, plus or minus 3%.

Nevertheless, Nvidia shares continued declining after the announcement.

The stock closed the November 19 regular trading session at $145.98, down 3.3% for the day. By the November 20 analysis snapshot, shares were indicated around $142.75.

The contrast offers an important lesson: strong corporate results do not automatically produce higher share prices.

Investors must also consider how much future growth is already reflected in a stock's valuation, whether margins can remain strong, and whether expectations for the AI industry will be fulfilled.

A stock trading substantially below its previous highs may offer a better entry price. But a lower share price does not automatically make it an undervalued investment.

For additional market context, see investingLive's analysis of the Nasdaq's reaction to Nvidia earnings.

Three potential buying prices, rather than one attempt to pick the bottom

Our illustrative strategy identifies three progressively lower prices at which an investor could consider purchasing Nvidia shares.

The first purchase at $139.56 represents the initial potential buying opportunity identified by our market analysis.

The second, at $136.07, allows for additional downside before increasing the position.

The third, at $130.27, is a deeper buying area intended for a scenario in which selling pressure continues.

These are proposed purchase prices, not confirmed support levels or predictions that Nvidia must trade there.

An investor buying 100 shares at each price would accumulate 300 shares with a total purchase cost of $40,590 and an average acquisition price of $135.30.

Importantly, 1X means buying the same number of shares at each level, not committing the same dollar amount.

The benefit of this approach is patience. The danger is accumulating more shares while the stock continues to weaken.

There is also no guarantee of execution. Nvidia could recover before reaching the first buying price, leaving the investor without a position.

That is an acceptable outcome for a strategy that prioritizes the entry price rather than immediate participation.

That is my patient 'buy the dip' plan. I might be wrong. Always do your own research and trade/invest at your own risk only.

The stop-loss level matters as much as the entry prices

The illustrative plan uses a common protective stop at $121.50.

If all three purchases execute, the average entry would be $135.30, creating an initial planned risk of:

  • $13.80 per share, approximately 10.2% of the average purchase price.

  • $4,140 for a completed 300-share position, assuming execution at the specified stop price.

This is a relatively wide stop. Investors who cannot tolerate that degree of price volatility, or who already hold substantial Nvidia exposure, may find the strategy unsuitable.

Buying more shares as prices fall increases exposure to further declines. A stop-loss order can help manage that exposure, but it does not guarantee execution at $121.50. A market gap or rapid selloff could produce a larger loss.

The stop is a risk-management reference, not a claim that Nvidia cannot fall further.

Four potential profit targets, from $157.70 to $223.50

If Nvidia eventually establishes a recovery, the strategy provides four potential profit-taking objectives.

The first target, $157.70, provides an opportunity to realize an initial gain rather than waiting for a much larger recovery.

The second target, $165.90, would require additional upward progress and offers another opportunity to reduce exposure.

The third target, $191.30, represents a more substantial recovery scenario.

The fourth target, $223.50, is an ambitious objective that would require a much stronger advance. It should not be interpreted as a price forecast or an equally likely outcome.

The reasoning behind dividing the position into four portions is straightforward: investors do not have to make an all-or-nothing decision at one exit price.

Partial profit-taking allows some gains to be realized while preserving exposure if a more sustained recovery develops.

The theoretical 3.57:1 reward-to-risk ratio, explained

Assuming all three purchases execute at their proposed prices, the average purchase price would be $135.30.

With 25% of the shares sold at each of the four targets, the average exit price, if all four targets execute as modeled, would be $184.60.

That produces the following hypothetical results for 300 shares:

In other words, the complete favorable scenario offers approximately $3.57 of gross potential profit for every $1 of planned initial risk.

However, this is not an expected return, probability of success or backtested performance result.

It assumes all three purchases and all four profit-taking orders execute at the proposed prices, without an intervening stop-out. Trading costs, slippage and taxes are excluded.

Actual results will differ if only some buy orders execute, targets are missed, or the position is stopped out.

An optional way to protect the position after the first profit target

If Nvidia reaches the first profit target at $157.70, an investor may consider two additional adjustments.

Move the stop to the actual average entry price.

After selling 25% of the acquired shares at TP1, the investor could move the protective stop on the remaining 75% to the position's weighted-average purchase price.

If all three entries executed, that reference would be $135.30.

But if only one or two purchases executed, the actual average would be different. The stop should reflect the shares genuinely acquired, not an assumed entry price.

Cancel any outstanding purchase orders.

Once the stock has advanced to TP1, the original buying opportunity may have changed.

Canceling any unfilled lower buy orders could help prevent new shares from being purchased unexpectedly if Nvidia subsequently declines.

What would this accomplish?

Consider the hypothetical 300-share position with an average entry of $135.30.

Selling 75 shares at $157.70 would produce a gross realized profit of $1,680.

If the remaining 225 shares were subsequently stopped out at exactly $135.30, their gross trading result would be zero, leaving the $1,680 profit from TP1 before costs.

That illustrates the benefit of reducing the remaining planned downside risk after taking an initial profit.

However, the adjustment introduces another trade-off.

Nvidia could retreat to the average purchase price, trigger the new stop, and subsequently resume climbing toward the higher targets. In that scenario, moving the stop to breakeven would have prevented participation in the larger recovery.

Execution costs and slippage can also turn a nominally breakeven stop into a loss on the remaining shares. Price gaps can create even larger deviations.

Important: The original 3.57:1 reward-to-risk calculation remains the theoretical all-targets-hit scenario. Introducing an optional breakeven stop changes the possible realized outcomes. That calculation does not incorporate the effects of this management decision on the path of the trade.

There is no universally correct point at which to move a protective stop. This is one potential management technique, not a compulsory rule.

What if Nvidia doesn't follow the plan?

Several outcomes are worth considering before committing capital.

Nvidia rebounds without reaching $139.56. No shares are purchased. The investor misses the recovery but avoids taking a position at a less favorable price than planned.

Only one or two buy orders execute. The position is smaller, and its actual average purchase price, capital at risk and potential reward-to-risk ratio must be recalculated.

All three entries execute before another significant decline. The strategy reaches its full intended exposure, and the $121.50 stop becomes particularly important. The fact that Nvidia reached progressively lower buying areas provides no assurance of a recovery.

Nvidia begins recovering and reaches some, but not all, targets. Partial profit-taking or the optional protective-stop adjustment can change the ultimate result considerably.

These possibilities demonstrate why a good-looking theoretical reward-to-risk ratio is only one part of evaluating an investment strategy.

What about investors who already own Nvidia?

An existing shareholder faces a somewhat different decision.

Buying additional shares at lower prices can reduce the average acquisition cost, but it increases overall exposure to Nvidia and its business-specific risks.

Someone who already has a large allocation to Nvidia or the AI sector might decide against adding more, regardless of how attractive the proposed entry prices appear.

A long-term investor also needs to assess the underlying business, expected growth, valuation and investment horizon separately from this price-based strategy.

The proposed stop and partial profit-taking structure represent one approach to managing a position. They are not necessarily appropriate for an investor intending to hold Nvidia for several years through substantial volatility.

The lesson: Plan the downside before pursuing the upside

Nvidia could recover strongly, continue declining, or remain volatile for an extended period.

The three-entry strategy does not attempt to predict which outcome will occur or precisely when the stock might bottom.

Its purpose is to show how investors can prepare for several possibilities: where they might consider buying, how much exposure they would take, how they would define an unsuccessful position, and how they might manage a recovery.

A patient strategy comes with a cost. Attractive limit orders sometimes remain unfilled, while filled orders can still lead to losses.

For investors, accepting those possibilities in advance may be more useful than trying to identify the perfect moment to buy.

Educational only. Trade at your own risk. This is an illustrative strategy, not personalized investment advice. No orders or executions are implied.
